anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data structures and index layout do not match workload access patterns, forcing even well-written SQL to scan or probe data inefficiently.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses a sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics, often because of cost-model or plan-cache issues.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Total memory consumed by caches, work areas, and processes exceeds safe limits, leading to pressure, paging, or OOM situations.

Composite definition: This anomaly represents the simultaneous presence of all three root causes—mis-designed schema/indexing, misguided plan selection, and runaway memory allocation—so the workload is forced down inefficient access paths, executed with poor plans, and starved for stable memory at the same time.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Full-table or wide index scans chosen over selective access cascade into large hash joins and sorts that inflate per-query work memory. Plan instability causes identical statements to alternate between memory-heavy and memory-light plans, inflating the plan cache while spilling to disk when memory pressure peaks. Buffer-cache churn grows because unfiltered scans evict useful pages, lowering hit ratios; concurrent sessions encounter paging, CPU stalls, or even OOM terminations. Latency can fluctuate wildly—sometimes dominated by I/O from scans, other times by memory spills or swap—making performance regressions hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causal chain: Poor schema and index design enlarges the data volume each plan must touch. When the optimizer mistakenly favors scan-heavy or join-order-unfriendly plans, it magnifies the I/O and CPU load generated by that sub-optimal physical design. The resulting oversized result sets and intermediate hash/sort structures consume excessive work memory, bloating global caches and per-session areas. Escalating memory pressure, in turn, destabilizes the optimizer (e.g., memory-aware plan suppression, plan cache evictions) and can further discourage index-based strategies, reinforcing the cycle. Thus, each root cause amplifies the others, leading to a converging spiral of inefficient access, bad plans, and memory exhaustion that degrades both throughput and predictability across OLTP and analytical queries.

entry.official_definition: The number of seconds that the mysqld server waits for a connect packet before responding with Bad handshake.
entry.trigger_condition: A client does not complete the initial connection packet exchange within connect_timeout.
entry.workload_impact: The connection attempt fails during handshake.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
